per_task.text: In the fictional opinion piece "The Quiet Desk", the author reflects on how artificial intelligence is changing office work and what may be lost in the process. Although the author acknowledges that many colleagues welcome the new tools for removing tedious routine tasks, they fear that something valuable, apparently the everyday exchange between colleagues, is disappearing along with the drudgery. The author also doubts economists' claim that technology creates more jobs than it destroys, arguing that long-term statistics offer little comfort to graduates who need work now. Their main concern, however, is the loss of apprenticeship: if machines take over simple tasks, junior employees lose the chance to learn their profession. Instead of rejecting technology, the author calls for deliberate decisions about which skills to preserve and warns that companies using AI only to cut costs risk losing experienced staff in the future.
why_effective: Covers all five main points in the text's order
Simple present, own words, no quotations

per_task.text:
The author develops their concerns gradually, which makes them appear balanced rather than alarmist. The text opens with a personal observation of an office that "grows a little quieter" every morning. This first-person perspective creates familiarity and invites readers to compare the scene with their own workplace, while the questions that follow ("Where is the latest version? Who has the client's number?") recreate the former atmosphere so that the reader senses what has been lost.

Instead of dismissing the opposing view, the author concedes that colleagues "point out, quite rightly," that nobody misses repetitive tasks. Only then does the contrastive "Yet" introduce doubts. This concession strengthens the author's credibility, because the criticism seems to come from someone who has considered both sides.

The central argument is supported by a vivid metaphor and a rhetorical question: "If the first rung of the ladder is removed, how is anyone supposed to climb?" The image makes the abstract problem of lost training opportunities concrete, and the question leaves readers to draw the uncomfortable conclusion themselves. Similarly, the colleague's remark that "nobody lives in the long run" exposes the gap between reassuring statistics and individual experience.

Finally, the text returns to the quiet office, creating a frame. The closing contrast between "efficient" and "healthy" turns a description into a question of values and stresses that the outcome depends on "choices we have barely begun to make".
why_effective: Each feature: example + effect + link to the warning
Follows the structure of the text

per_task.text:
Few people would object to software that saves time and money. Yet the view that companies treating AI "merely as a way to cut costs" will only profit in the short term deserves serious consideration, because it raises the question of what makes a business successful over time.

On the one hand, it is understandable that firms look at costs first. Small businesses in particular often operate on tight margins, and automating routine tasks can decide whether they survive a difficult year. From this perspective, refusing to use AI for savings would be naive.

On the other hand, a strategy based only on savings overlooks how expertise is built. Experienced employees did not acquire their judgement from training courses alone but from years of routine work, mistakes and feedback. If entry-level tasks disappear and nothing replaces them, companies may soon find that nobody is ready to take over when senior staff retire. Moreover, employees who feel they are merely being replaced are unlikely to show the commitment and creativity that technology cannot provide.

The more convincing approach is therefore not to choose between efficiency and people but to combine them. A firm could, for instance, use AI for repetitive data entry while giving junior staff responsibility for checking results and dealing with clients, so that they still learn the business.

All in all, the view is largely persuasive: cutting costs with AI is legitimate, but companies that see it only as a savings tool risk exchanging a short-term gain for a long-term loss of skills.
why_effective: Concrete example in the solution paragraph

alternative_interpretations: Task 2 could also centre on tone: the calm, reflective voice itself persuades by contrast with alarmist debates about AI.
Task 3 could reasonably disagree, for example by arguing that markets will force firms to train staff once skills become scarce.
